mn01-veltliner.title: Grüner Veltliner?
mn01-veltliner.body: {gäst} at table {bord} points at the drinks list: "Grüner Veltliner. What is that, exactly?"

steps.question: What is Grüner Veltliner?

a.label: A white grape, Austria's most planted
a.explanation: Grüner Veltliner is a white grape and Austria's most planted variety, grown above all along the Danube in Lower Austria: the Wachau, Kamptal and Kremstal.

b.label: A red grape from Germany
b.explanation: It is a white grape, and its home is Austria, not Germany.

c.label: A blend of several grapes from the Alps
c.explanation: Grüner Veltliner is a single grape variety, and the wine on the list is made from it alone.

fail.outcome: {personal} guesses at an answer. The guest nods politely, unconvinced.

steps.question: At what temperature do you serve it?

a.label: Well chilled, about 8–10 °C
a.explanation: A fresh, crisp white is served chilled. At 8–10 °C the acidity and the peppery note that Grüner Veltliner is known for come through.

b.label: Ice-cold, 2–4 °C, straight from the freezer
b.explanation: So cold that the aroma closes up. The guest tastes cold, not wine.

c.label: Room temperature, 18–20 °C
c.explanation: Too warm for a fresh white wine: the alcohol takes over and the crisp acidity goes flat.

fail.outcome: The glass arrives at the wrong temperature. The guest sips and pushes it aside.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, putting it right, while other tables wait.

steps.question: What on the menu goes best with it?

a.label: Only the dessert
a.explanation: A dry white wine tastes sour next to something sweet. Dessert wants a sweeter wine.

b.label: Light dishes: fish, vegetables, the chanterelles
b.explanation: A fresh, light white wine suits light food. Its acidity lifts fish and vegetables without drowning them.

c.label: The game, the richest and heaviest plate we have tonight
c.explanation: Venison wants a wine with more body, such as a red. A light white disappears next to it.

fail.outcome: The guest orders something that does not suit the wine, and it shows.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, smoothing things over, while other tables wait.

success.outcome: The guest orders another glass and asks {personal} for the name of the producer.

staff.outcome: {personal} takes over and recommends something at random. The guest drinks without much joy.
staff.ongoing: {personal} is tied up at table {bord}, and the other tables wait longer.

mn02-pinot.title: The Pinot Noir
mn02-pinot.body: {gäst} at table {bord} is choosing between the reds: "Tell me about the Pinot Noir."

steps.question: Where does Pinot Noir have its classic home?

a.label: Burgundy, in France
a.explanation: Pinot Noir is the red grape of Burgundy, where the great red wines are made from it alone. It is also grown in Champagne, Germany, Oregon and New Zealand.

b.label: Rioja, in Spain
b.explanation: Rioja's red wines are made mainly from Tempranillo, not Pinot Noir.

c.label: The Douro, in northern Portugal
c.explanation: The Douro is the home of port, made from grapes such as Touriga Nacional.

fail.outcome: {personal} mixes up the regions. The guest knows better and says so.

steps.question: How do you serve Pinot Noir?

a.label: Warm, about 22 °C, so that it opens up
a.explanation: At 22 °C the alcohol dominates and the wine tastes heavy. Room temperature is warmer today than when the rule was made.

b.label: Straight from the fridge, about 5 °C
b.explanation: Too cold for a red: the fruit closes up and the tannins feel harsher.

c.label: Slightly cool, about 14–16 °C, in a wide glass
c.explanation: A light red gains from being a little cool: the fruit stays fresh and the alcohol in the background. A wide bowl gathers the aroma.

fail.outcome: The wine arrives too warm. The guest waits for it to cool.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, putting it right, while other tables wait.

steps.question: Which dish on tonight's menu goes with it?

a.label: Nothing: a good red is best drunk entirely without food
a.explanation: Pinot Noir is one of the most food-friendly reds. Saying no loses a sale and a good pairing.

b.label: The earthy dishes: lamb, game or the chanterelles
b.explanation: Pinot Noir has red berries and an earthy, forest-floor character. It suits lamb, game and mushrooms without drowning them.

c.label: The lingonberry sorbet
c.explanation: A tart, sweet sorbet makes a dry red wine taste thin and bitter.

fail.outcome: The guest shrugs and orders the house wine instead.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, smoothing things over, while other tables wait.

success.outcome: The guest orders the bottle for the table and thanks {personal} for the advice.

staff.outcome: {personal} takes over. The advice is vague and the guest settles for a glass.
staff.ongoing: {personal} is tied up at table {bord}, and the other tables wait longer.

mn03-gos.title: The pike-perch
mn03-gos.body: {gäst} at table {bord} looks at the menu: "Poached pike-perch. Is it a local fish?"

steps.question: What is pike-perch?

a.label: A freshwater fish of the perch family, from Hjälmaren
a.explanation: Pike-perch (zander) is a freshwater fish of the perch family, with firm white flesh. Hjälmaren, a lake south of Grythyttan, is known for it.

b.label: A saltwater fish caught in the North Sea and frozen on board the boat
b.explanation: Pike-perch lives in lakes and slow rivers, and in the brackish water of the Baltic, not the salty North Sea.

c.label: A farmed salmon
c.explanation: Salmon has pink, fatty flesh. Pike-perch is a lean white fish, and ours is caught in the lake.

fail.outcome: {personal} is not sure where the fish comes from. The guest orders something else.

steps.question: How is it poached so it stays juicy?

a.label: At a rolling boil for ten minutes
a.explanation: Far too hard and long: the fish falls apart and turns dry and stringy.

b.label: Poached early in the morning and then reheated when it is ordered
b.explanation: Reheated fish loses its texture and can be a food-safety risk if it has stood warm.

c.label: Just below a simmer, about 80 °C, for a few minutes
c.explanation: Gentle heat keeps the delicate flesh together and juicy. A rolling boil tears it apart and dries it out.

fail.outcome: The fish comes out dry. The guest leaves half of it.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, putting it right, while other tables wait.

steps.question: Another guest at the table is allergic to fish. What do you answer when they ask if the kitchen can keep things apart?

a.label: Say that freshwater fish does not count
a.explanation: A fish allergy usually covers freshwater fish too. It is not true, and it is dangerous.

b.label: Ask the kitchen and honestly say what can be promised
b.explanation: With allergies, honesty comes first. The kitchen knows about shared pans and oil. A promise you cannot keep is a risk to the guest.

c.label: Say it will be fine, without first asking the kitchen about the fish
c.explanation: An unchecked promise about an allergy can make a guest seriously ill.

fail.outcome: The table grows uneasy. They order little and leave early.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, smoothing things over, while other tables wait.

success.outcome: The guest orders the pike-perch and asks {personal} to thank the kitchen.

staff.outcome: {personal} takes over, but the answers are vague. The table orders the cheapest dish.
staff.ongoing: {personal} is tied up at table {bord}, and the other tables wait longer.

mn04-kantareller.title: The chanterelles
mn04-kantareller.body: {gäst} at table {bord} reads the menu aloud: "Chanterelles on toast. Are they from around here?"

steps.question: What are chanterelles?

a.label: Wild forest mushrooms, picked in late summer
a.explanation: Chanterelles grow wild in Swedish forests, in moss near birch and spruce. The season runs from July into autumn, and they are not cultivated.

b.label: Cultivated button mushrooms from a mushroom farm nearby
b.explanation: Button mushrooms are grown indoors. Chanterelles are picked wild in the forest.

c.label: A kind of truffle imported from Italy
c.explanation: Truffles grow underground and are something else. Chanterelles are golden mushrooms found above the moss.

fail.outcome: {personal} does not know what they are. The guest loses interest.

steps.question: How are chanterelles cleaned in the kitchen?

a.label: Soaked in water for an hour
a.explanation: Soaked chanterelles boil in their own water instead of frying, and the flavour goes flat.

b.label: Not at all, the forest soil gives flavour
b.explanation: Soil and needles grate between the teeth. The flavour is in the mushroom, not the dirt.

c.label: With a brush or small knife, as dry as possible
c.explanation: Chanterelles soak up water and go soggy in the pan. Brush off soil and needles, and trim the stem.

fail.outcome: The chanterelles come out soggy and gritty.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, putting it right, while other tables wait.

steps.question: A guest with coeliac disease wants the chanterelles. What do you say?

a.label: Scrape off the butter
a.explanation: Butter contains lactose, not gluten. The problem is the bread.

b.label: Say the toast contains gluten, and offer another dish or the mushrooms without bread
b.explanation: Coeliac disease means no gluten at all. The toast is wheat. Say so clearly, and ask the kitchen what can be served safely.

c.label: Serve it, a little bread is fine
c.explanation: For someone with coeliac disease even a small amount of gluten causes harm.

fail.outcome: The guest gets the wrong answer and does not trust the menu after that.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, smoothing things over, while other tables wait.

success.outcome: The guest orders the chanterelles and takes a photo of the plate.

staff.outcome: {personal} takes over. The guest orders, but without much enthusiasm.

mn05-linser.title: Is it vegan?
mn05-linser.body: {gäst} at table {bord} is vegan and asks about the roast roots with lentils.

steps.question: Is the dish vegan?

a.label: Yes: lentils, root vegetables and herbs, nothing from animals
a.explanation: The dish is lentils, root vegetables and herbs. Lentils are legumes and a good source of protein, so the plate is filling without meat or dairy.

b.label: No, lentils count as a dairy product and contain milk protein
b.explanation: Lentils are legumes, seeds of a plant. They have nothing to do with dairy.

c.label: Only if the cream is left out
c.explanation: There is no cream in the dish. Guessing makes the guest doubt the whole answer.

fail.outcome: The guest is unsure what is in the dish and orders only a drink.

steps.question: How are the lentils cooked?

a.label: Soaked overnight and boiled hard for two hours
a.explanation: That turns lentils to mush. It is how some dried beans are treated, not lentils.

b.label: Served raw for the crunch
b.explanation: Raw lentils are hard to digest and not eaten as they are.

c.label: Rinsed and simmered gently until tender, no soaking needed
c.explanation: Unlike dried beans, lentils need no soaking. Rinse them and simmer gently so they hold their shape.

fail.outcome: The lentils come out mushy.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, putting it right, while other tables wait.

steps.question: The vegan guest asks for a dessert. What do you suggest?

a.label: Say there is nothing vegan at all and bring the bill straight away
a.explanation: It loses a sale and the guest leaves feeling unwelcome, when there was an option.

b.label: Check the list: sorbet is just berries; the cream dessert isn't vegan
b.explanation: The lingonberry sorbet has no cream or egg. The cream dessert has both. Knowing the list saves the guest a question.

c.label: The cream dessert, it is light
c.explanation: Cream and egg are animal products. Light is not the same as vegan.

fail.outcome: The guest skips dessert and leaves.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, smoothing things over, while other tables wait.

success.outcome: The guest orders the lentils and says they will come back with friends.

staff.outcome: {personal} takes over and answers carefully, but the guest remains doubtful.
staff.ongoing: {personal} is tied up at table {bord}, and the other tables wait longer.

mn06-lingon.title: Lingonberries
mn06-lingon.body: {gäst} at table {bord} is visiting from abroad and has spotted lingonberries on the list: "What are those?"

steps.question: What are lingonberries?

a.label: A wild Nordic heather-family berry, tart and red
a.explanation: Lingonberries grow wild in Nordic forests, on a low evergreen shrub of the heather family. They are red and tart.

b.label: A cultivated strawberry variety
b.explanation: Lingonberries are small, wild and tart. Strawberries are another plant.

c.label: A citrus fruit imported from Spain in winter, sweet and yellow
c.explanation: They are a Nordic forest berry, not a citrus fruit.

fail.outcome: {personal} fumbles the answer. The guest orders what they know.

steps.question: Why do lingonberries keep so well?

a.label: They are always frozen
a.explanation: Many are frozen, but the reason they keep even raw is the benzoic acid.

b.label: They contain a lot of sugar
b.explanation: Lingonberries are tart, with little sugar. It is the acid that keeps them.

c.label: They contain natural benzoic acid, which preserves them
c.explanation: Lingonberries contain benzoic acid, a natural preservative. That is why raw-stirred lingonberries keep without cooking.

fail.outcome: The guest gets a muddled answer and loses interest.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, putting it right, while other tables wait.

steps.question: The guest does not drink alcohol. What should they have with the meal?

a.label: Just a small glass of wine, it is almost nothing for an adult
a.explanation: A guest who does not drink alcohol means none. Pushing it is disrespectful.

b.label: The alcohol-free lingonberry sparkling: tart and fresh, like a wine with food
b.explanation: Acidity is what makes a drink work with food. A tart, sparkling lingonberry drink does the job of a wine without alcohol.

c.label: Water only, we have nothing else
c.explanation: It is not true if the list has an alcohol-free drink, and it loses a sale.

fail.outcome: The guest drinks water and leaves without dessert.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, smoothing things over, while other tables wait.

success.outcome: The guest orders the lingonberry drink and the sorbet, and asks where to pick lingonberries.

staff.outcome: {personal} takes over and points at the list. The guest orders water.
staff.ongoing: {personal} is tied up at table {bord}, and the other tables wait longer.

mn07-soppan.title: The soup
mn07-soppan.body: {gäst} at table {bord} cannot tolerate lactose and asks about the root vegetable soup.

steps.question: What makes the soup creamy?

a.label: Cream, so it contains lactose
a.explanation: The soup is finished with cream, a dairy product, so it contains lactose.

b.label: Only the root vegetables, so it is lactose-free
b.explanation: The recipe has cream. Saying it is lactose-free is wrong and harms the guest.

c.label: Coconut milk
c.explanation: Not in this soup. Guessing about ingredients is a risk with intolerances.

fail.outcome: {personal} is not sure what is in the soup. The guest orders nothing.

steps.question: How do you bring out the sweetness of the root vegetables?

a.label: Boil them for a long time in plenty of water
a.explanation: Long boiling leaches flavour into the water and gives no browning.

b.label: Add sugar at the end
b.explanation: It makes the soup sweet, not deep. Roasting gives the roots' own sweetness.

c.label: Roast them at high heat, about 200 °C, until the surface browns
c.explanation: At high heat the surface browns and caramelises, and the natural sugars in the roots taste sweeter and deeper.

fail.outcome: The soup tastes thin.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, putting it right, while other tables wait.

steps.question: What do you suggest for the guest who cannot tolerate lactose?

a.label: Say the lactose disappears if the soup is heated more
a.explanation: Heating does not remove lactose. It is simply not true.

b.label: Say the soup has cream, and suggest a lactose-free dish such as the lentils
b.explanation: Be clear about the cream and offer something the guest can eat. The lentils have no dairy.

c.label: Say it is only a little cream
c.explanation: A little cream still contains lactose. The guest decides, and needs the truth.

fail.outcome: The guest orders the soup, trusting the answer, and regrets it.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, smoothing things over, while other tables wait.

success.outcome: The guest orders the lentils and thanks {personal} for being clear.

staff.outcome: {personal} takes over. The guest gets an answer, but feels unsure.

mn08-flaskan.title: A bottle for the table
mn08-flaskan.body: A party of four at table {bord} want a glass or two each. {gäst} asks: "Glasses or a bottle?"

steps.question: How many glasses does a 75 cl bottle give?

a.label: About five glasses of 15 cl
a.explanation: A standard serving is about 15 cl, so a 75 cl bottle gives five glasses.

b.label: Two glasses
b.explanation: That would be glasses of almost 40 cl each, far more than a serving.

c.label: Ten glasses
c.explanation: That would be 7.5 cl each, a tasting pour rather than a glass.

fail.outcome: {personal} gets the numbers wrong. The table orders single glasses.

steps.question: How do you open the bottle at the table?

a.label: Open it at the bar and pour for the whole table straight away, to save time
a.explanation: The guest never sees the bottle or tastes it first. A faulty bottle ends up in every glass.

b.label: Pop the cork loudly for effect
b.explanation: A still wine is opened quietly. A bang belongs to nothing on this list.

c.label: Show the label, cut below the lip, draw the cork quietly, host tastes first
c.explanation: The guest sees they got what they ordered, the wine does not touch the capsule, and the host checks the wine before everyone is poured.

fail.outcome: The bottle is opened clumsily and the host frowns.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, putting it right, while other tables wait.

steps.question: What do you suggest for the party?

a.label: A bottle each
a.explanation: Four bottles is twenty glasses for four people. Upselling that far loses trust.

b.label: A bottle: five glasses cost less than five by the glass, and the table shares
b.explanation: On our list a bottle costs less than five single glasses. For a table of four it is better value and a nicer moment.

c.label: Four glasses of four different wines, always, so everyone at the table gets to try something
c.explanation: It can be fun, but the table asked for value, and it costs them more.

fail.outcome: The table orders glass by glass and the bill surprises them.

success.outcome: The table orders a bottle and a second one later.

mn09-olet.title: The local beer
mn09-olet.body: {gäst} at table {bord} would rather have a beer: "Is the beer local?"

steps.question: Where does tonight's beer come from?

a.label: The brewery in Nora, a short drive from Grythyttan
a.explanation: The beer comes from the brewery in Nora, the neighbouring town. Local suppliers are part of the story the guest pays for.

b.label: Imported from Belgium
b.explanation: Not tonight's beer. Getting the origin wrong undermines the local story.

c.label: Brewed in our own kitchen, in small batches every week in season
c.explanation: The wine bar does not brew. The Brewpub has its own brewery; we buy from Nora.

fail.outcome: {personal} guesses wrong about the beer. The guest notices.

steps.question: How do you pour the beer into the glass?

a.label: Straight down, fast, into the middle
a.explanation: The glass fills with foam, the beer goes flat and the guest waits.

b.label: Into a warm glass straight from the dishwasher, so the beer is not too cold
b.explanation: A warm glass makes the beer foam over and warm up.

c.label: Tilt the glass, pour down the side, then straighten it for a small head
c.explanation: Pouring down the side keeps the carbonation, and straightening at the end builds a head that carries the aroma.

fail.outcome: The beer arrives flat and foamy at the same time.
fail.ongoing: {personal} is still at table {bord}, putting it right, while other tables wait.

steps.question: The guest having the pork asks: wine or beer?

a.label: Only the most expensive wine will do
a.explanation: The guest asked for advice, not a sales pitch.

b.label: Either works: a malty beer suits pork and roots, and costs less
b.explanation: Pork with roasted roots suits the malt in a beer as well as a fresh wine. Give the guest a real choice.

c.label: Beer never goes with food in a wine bar; wine is what the guests came for
c.explanation: Beer is an excellent food drink, and it is on our list for a reason.

fail.outcome: The guest feels steered and orders nothing more.

success.outcome: The guest orders a beer and a second one with dessert.
